title: Part 6, Chapter 1
paragraphs: A strange period began for Raskolnikov. It was as though a fog had descended on him, wrapping him in a lonely, dreary isolation from which there was no escape. Looking back on it later, he believed his mind had been clouded at times, with occasional lucid intervals, right up until the final catastrophe. He was certain he had been mistaken about many things during this time — about the timing of events, for example. In any case, when he later tried to piece his memories together, much of what he learned about himself came from other people. He had confused incidents, had attributed events to circumstances that existed only in his imagination. At times he was gripped by agonizing, morbid anxiety, sometimes rising to outright panic. But he also remembered moments, hours, perhaps whole days of complete apathy — a reaction to the preceding terror that resembled the abnormal numbness sometimes seen in the dying. In that state he seemed to be deliberately avoiding a full, clear understanding of his situation. Certain essential facts that demanded immediate attention were especially unbearable to him. How gladly he would have freed himself from certain worries — yet neglecting them threatened complete and inevitable ruin.

He was particularly worried about Svidrigailov — one could even say Svidrigailov occupied his thoughts constantly. From the moment of Svidrigailov's all-too-threatening and unmistakable words in Sonia's room, at the time of Katerina Ivanovna's death, the normal workings of his mind seemed to have broken down. Yet although this new fact caused him extreme anxiety, Raskolnikov was in no hurry to confront it. Sometimes, finding himself in some remote, desolate part of the city, in some wretched eating-house, sitting alone and lost in thought, barely knowing how he'd gotten there, he would suddenly think of Svidrigailov. He would recognize with sudden, alarming clarity that he needed to come to terms with that man as soon as possible, to make whatever deal he could. Once, walking outside the city limits, he even convinced himself they had arranged to meet there, that he was waiting for Svidrigailov. Another time he woke before dawn lying on the ground under some bushes, unable to understand how he'd ended up there.

During the two or three days after Katerina Ivanovna's death, he had encountered Svidrigailov two or three times at Sonia's lodgings, where he'd gone aimlessly, just for a moment. They exchanged a few words but never touched on the critical subject, as though they had tacitly agreed to leave it aside for the time being.

Katerina Ivanovna's body was still lying in the coffin. Svidrigailov was busy arranging the funeral. Sonia was very busy too. At their last meeting, Svidrigailov told Raskolnikov he had made arrangements — very satisfactory ones — for Katerina Ivanovna's children. Through certain connections he had managed to reach the right people, and the three orphans could be immediately placed in excellent institutions. The money he had settled on them helped greatly, since it's much easier to place orphans who have some means than destitute ones. He also said something about Sonia and promised to come see Raskolnikov in a day or two, mentioning that "he'd like to discuss something, that there were things they needed to talk about..."

This conversation took place in the hallway on the stairs. Svidrigailov looked intently at Raskolnikov, and after a brief pause, lowered his voice: "What's wrong, Rodion Romanovitch? You don't seem like yourself. You look and listen, but it's as if you don't understand. Pull yourself together! We'll talk things over; I'm just sorry I'm so busy with my own affairs and other people's. Ah, Rodion Romanovitch," he added suddenly, "what every person needs is fresh air — fresh air... more than anything!"

He stepped aside to let the priest and his assistant pass on the stairs. They had come for the requiem service. By Svidrigailov's orders, it was sung twice a day, punctually. Svidrigailov went on his way. Raskolnikov stood still a moment, thought, then followed the priest into Sonia's room. He stood by the door. The service began: quiet, slow, mournful. Since childhood, the thought of death and its presence had always felt oppressive and mysteriously terrible to him; and it had been a long time since he'd last heard a requiem service. There was something else here too — something awful and disturbing. He looked at the children: they were all kneeling by the coffin; Polenka was crying. Behind them, Sonia prayed, weeping softly and — it seemed — timidly.

"She hasn't said a word to me these past two days — she hasn't even glanced at me," Raskolnikov thought. The sunlight was bright in the room; clouds of incense rose; the priest intoned: "Grant rest, O Lord..." Raskolnikov stayed through the entire service. As the priest blessed them and took his leave, he looked around with a strange expression. After the service, Raskolnikov went up to Sonia. She took both his hands and rested her head on his shoulder. This small, friendly gesture puzzled Raskolnikov. It struck him as strange that there was no trace of revulsion, no sign of disgust, no trembling in her hand. It was the ultimate act of self-sacrifice — at least that's how he interpreted it.

Sonia said nothing. Raskolnikov pressed her hand and left. He felt utterly wretched. If he could have escaped to some wilderness, he would have considered himself lucky — even if it meant spending his whole life there. But although he had been almost entirely alone lately, he had never managed to feel truly alone. Sometimes he would walk out of the city onto the highway; once he even reached a small woods. But the lonelier the place, the more aware he became of some uneasy presence nearby. It didn't frighten him, but it annoyed him intensely, so he would hurry back to the city, lose himself in the crowds, duck into restaurants and taverns, walk through the busiest streets. There he felt easier and, paradoxically, more solitary. One evening at dusk he sat for an hour in a tavern listening to songs, and he remembered that he actually enjoyed it. But suddenly the same unease returned, as though his conscience were pricking him. "Here I sit listening to songs — is that what I ought to be doing?" he thought. Yet he immediately sensed that wasn't the only cause; there was something demanding an immediate decision, but he couldn't put it into words or even think it through clearly. It was a hopeless tangle. "No — better to fight again! Better Porfiry again... or Svidrigailov... Better some challenge, some attack. Yes, yes!" he thought. He left the tavern and practically broke into a run. The thought of Dunya and his mother suddenly filled him with something close to panic. That night he woke before dawn among some bushes on Krestovsky Island, shivering with fever. He walked home; it was early morning when he arrived. After a few hours' sleep the fever passed, but he woke up late — two in the afternoon.

He remembered that Katerina Ivanovna's funeral was scheduled for that day, and he was glad he hadn't attended. Nastasya brought him food; he ate and drank eagerly, almost greedily. His head was clearer and he felt calmer than he had in three days. He even felt a passing wonder at his previous attacks of panic.
The door opened and Razumikhin came in.
"Ah — he's eating, so he's not sick," said Razumikhin. He pulled up a chair and sat down across the table from Raskolnikov.
He was troubled and made no attempt to hide it. He spoke with obvious irritation, but without hurrying or raising his voice. He seemed to have some specific, firm purpose in mind.

"Listen," he began decisively. "As far as I'm concerned, you can all go to hell, but from what I can see, it's obvious I can't make head or tail of any of this. Please don't think I've come to interrogate you. I don't want to know — to hell with it! If you start telling me your secrets, I probably won't even stay to listen — I'll just walk out cursing. I've come for one thing only: to find out once and for all whether you're insane. There's a conviction floating around that you're mad or close to it. I'll admit I was leaning that way myself, judging by your stupid, repulsive, and completely inexplicable behavior — and from your recent treatment of your mother and sister. Only a monster or a madman could treat them the way you have. So you must be mad."
"When did you last see them?"

"Just now. Haven't you seen them since? Where have you been? Tell me, please — I've been to your room three times already. Your mother has been seriously ill since yesterday. She was determined to come to you; Avdotya Romanovna tried to stop her, but she wouldn't listen. 'If he's sick, if he's losing his mind, who should look after him if not his mother?' she said. We all came together — we couldn't let her come alone. We begged her to stay calm the whole way. We arrived, and you weren't here. She sat down, waited ten minutes while we stood there in silence. Then she got up and said: 'If he's gone out — meaning he's well enough — and has forgotten his mother, then it's humiliating and improper for his mother to stand at his door begging for kindness.' She went home and took to her bed; now she has a fever. 'I see,' she said, 'that he has time for his girl.' She means Sofya Semyonovna by 'your girl' — your fiancée or your mistress, I don't know which. I went straight to Sofya Semyonovna's myself, wanting to find out what was going on. I looked around — there was the coffin, the children crying, Sofya Semyonovna trying mourning clothes on them. No sign of you. I apologized, left, and reported back to Avdotya Romanovna. So that's all nonsense — you don't have any girl. The likeliest explanation is that you're mad. But here you sit, wolfing down boiled beef as though you haven't eaten in three days. Then again, mad people eat too. But even though you haven't said a word to me... you're not mad! I'd stake anything on it. So you can all go to hell — there's some mystery here, some secret, and I have no intention of racking my brains over your secrets. I've just come to blow off steam," he finished, rising. "To get it off my chest. And now I know what to do."
"What do you intend to do?"
"What business is it of yours?"
"You're going to go on a drinking binge."
"How... how did you know?"
"It's pretty obvious."
Razumikhin paused for a moment.
"You've always been a very rational person, and you've never been mad — never," he said suddenly with warmth. "You're right: I'll drink. Goodbye!"
He started for the door.
"I was talking with my sister about you — the day before yesterday, I think it was — Razumikhin."
"About me! But... where could you have seen her the day before yesterday?" Razumikhin stopped short and even turned slightly pale.
You could see that his heart was pounding — slowly, heavily.
"She came here by herself, sat there, and talked to me."
"She did!"
"Yes."
"What did you say to her... about me, I mean?"
"I told her you were a very good, honest, and hardworking man. I didn't tell her you love her, because she already knows."
"She knows?"

"Of course she does. Wherever I might go, whatever happens to me, you would stay to look after them. I'm entrusting them to your care, so to speak, Razumikhin. I say this because I know perfectly well how you feel about her, and I'm convinced your heart is pure. I also know she may love you too — perhaps she already does. Decide for yourself whether you need that drinking binge or not."

"Rodya! You see... well... damn it! Where are you planning to go? Look, if it's all some secret, fine, never mind... But I... I'll figure out the secret... and I'm sure it's just some ridiculous nonsense you've dreamed up. Anyway, you're a fine fellow — a really fine fellow!"

"What I was about to add — but you interrupted me — was that you made an excellent decision not to try to uncover those secrets. Let time sort it out. Don't worry about it. You'll learn everything when the time comes. Someone said to me yesterday that what a person needs is fresh air — fresh air. I'm about to go see him, to find out exactly what he meant by that."
Razumikhin stood lost in thought and excitement, working something out in silence.
"He's a political conspirator! He must be. And he's on the brink of some desperate step — that's certain. It can only be that! And... Dunya knows," he thought suddenly.

"So Avdotya Romanovna comes to visit you," he said, weighing each syllable, "and you're about to go see a man who says we need more air — and of course that letter... that must be connected somehow," he concluded to himself.
"What letter?"

"She received a letter today. It upset her terribly — far too much. I started talking about you, and she asked me not to. Then... then she said we might have to part very soon. Then she started thanking me warmly for something. Then she went to her room and locked herself in."
"She got a letter?" Raskolnikov asked thoughtfully.
"Yes. You didn't know? Hmm..."
They were both silent.
"Goodbye, Rodion. There was a time, brother, when I... Never mind. Goodbye. You see, there was a time... Well, goodbye! I have to go too. I'm not going to drink. No need now... That's all nonsense!"
He hurried out, but when he had nearly closed the door behind him, he suddenly opened it again and said, looking away:

"Oh, by the way — you know that murder case? Porfiry's case — the old woman? The murderer's been found: he's confessed and given them proof. It's one of those workmen — the house painter, can you imagine? Remember how I defended them here? Would you believe it — the whole scene of fighting and laughing with his co-workers on the stairs while the porter and those two witnesses were on their way up — he staged all of it on purpose, to throw off suspicion. The cunning, the nerve! Hard to believe — but it's his own confession, he admitted everything! What a fool I was to fall for it! But in my opinion he's simply a genius of deception and quick thinking — there's nothing all that surprising about it, I suppose. People like that do exist. And the fact that he couldn't keep it up and confessed actually makes his story more believable. But what a fool I was! I was passionately on their side!"
"Tell me, please — where did you hear this, and why does it interest you so much?" Raskolnikov asked with unmistakable agitation.
"What a question! You ask me why it interests me!... Well, I heard it from Porfiry, among others. In fact, I heard almost everything from him."
"From Porfiry?"
"From Porfiry."
"What... what did he say?" Raskolnikov asked in alarm.
"He gave me an excellent explanation. Psychological — in his usual way."
"He explained it? Explained it himself?"

"Yes, yes. Goodbye! I'll tell you the whole thing another time, but right now I'm busy. There was a time when I thought... But never mind — later! Why would I need to drink now? You've made me drunk without wine. I'm drunk, Rodya! Good-bye — I'm going. I'll come back soon."
He left.

"He's a political conspirator — there's no doubt about it," Razumikhin decided as he slowly descended the stairs. "And he's dragged his sister into it — that's entirely consistent with Avdotya Romanovna's character. They're having meetings!... She hinted as much. So many of her words, her hints — they all point that way! And how else can this whole tangle be explained? Hmm! And I was practically thinking... Good God, what I was thinking! Yes, I lost my mind and wronged him! It was his doing — that day under the lamp in the corridor. Pah! What a crude, vile, nasty idea of mine! Good for Nikolay, confessing... And how clear it all is now! His illness then, all his strange behavior... even before that, back at the university — so gloomy, so morose all the time... But what does that letter mean? Maybe there's something in that, too. Who was it from? I have my suspicions... No, I have to get to the bottom of this!"
He thought of Dunya, and everything he'd heard hit him with full force. His heart pounded, and he suddenly broke into a run.

As soon as Razumikhin left, Raskolnikov got up, went to the window, paced from one corner to the other as if forgetting how small his room was, then sat back down on the sofa. He felt — renewed, somehow. Again there was a fight, a way forward.

"Yes, a way forward had appeared! Things had been too suffocating, too crushing — the weight had been unbearable. A kind of paralysis had set in at times. From the moment of the scene with Nikolay at Porfiry's office, he had felt trapped, penned in without hope of escape. After Nikolay's confession — that very same day — the scene with Sonia had followed. His behavior and his final words had been nothing like what he'd imagined beforehand; he had weakened — instantly, fundamentally! And he had agreed with Sonia at the time, agreed in his heart that he couldn't go on living alone with such a thing on his conscience!

"And Svidrigailov was a riddle... He worried him, true, but somehow on a different level. He might still have a confrontation coming with Svidrigailov. Svidrigailov, too, might be a way out; but Porfiry was a different matter.

"So Porfiry himself had explained it to Razumikhin — had explained it psychologically! He was back to his damned psychology again! Porfiry? But to think that Porfiry could believe, even for a moment, that Nikolay was guilty — after everything that had passed between them before Nikolay's appearance, after that face-to-face conversation that could have only one explanation? During those days Raskolnikov had often replayed passages of that scene with Porfiry in his mind; he couldn't bear to dwell on it. Such words, such looks had been exchanged, things had been said in such a tone, and matters had gone so far that Nikolay — whom Porfiry had seen through from the first word, the first gesture — could not possibly have shaken his conviction.

"And to think that even Razumikhin had started to suspect! The scene in the corridor, under the lamp, had made its impression. He'd gone running to Porfiry... But why had Porfiry received him that way? What had been his purpose in diverting Razumikhin with Nikolay? He must have some plan, some scheme — but what? True, a long time had passed since that morning — too long — and there'd been no sight or sound of Porfiry. Well, that was a bad sign..."

Raskolnikov took his cap and went out, still pondering. It was the first time in a long while that his head had felt clear. "I have to deal with Svidrigailov," he thought, "and as soon as possible. He seems to be waiting for me to come to him on my own." At that moment such a surge of hatred rose in his exhausted heart that he could have killed either of them — Porfiry or Svidrigailov. At the very least, he felt he would be capable of it later, if not now.
"We'll see, we'll see," he repeated to himself.

But no sooner had he opened the door than he ran straight into Porfiry himself in the hallway. Porfiry was coming to see him. For a moment Raskolnikov was dumbfounded — but only for a moment. Strangely, he wasn't very surprised to see Porfiry, and he was barely afraid. He was merely startled, but quickly — instantly — on his guard. "Perhaps this means the end? But how had Porfiry crept up so quietly, like a cat, without making a sound? Could he have been listening at the door?"

"You weren't expecting a visitor, Rodion Romanovitch?" Porfiry explained, laughing. "I've been meaning to look in for a long time. I was passing by and thought — why not stop in for five minutes? Going out? I won't keep you. Just let me have one cigarette."
"Sit down, Porfiry Petrovitch, sit down." Raskolnikov offered his visitor a seat with such a pleased, friendly expression that he would have marveled at himself if he could have seen it.
The last moment had arrived. The final drops had to be drained! Just as a man might endure half an hour of mortal terror with a robber — yet when the knife is finally at his throat, he feels no fear.
Raskolnikov sat down directly facing Porfiry and looked at him without flinching. Porfiry squinted and began lighting a cigarette.
"Speak! Speak!" seemed ready to burst from Raskolnikov's chest. "Well? Why won't you speak?"
